⬇ Offline

…

This app holds the offline capability, so the platform serves a scope-confined service worker at /app/ and injects its registration. The capability buys exactly one thing — cold boot, the document and its assets answering with no network. Everything else below an app already has ungranted; the probes exist to show you which half is which.

1 · Worker registration

Registered by the platform, not by app code — there is no service worker in this bundle. The scope is the manifest's, and it can never be /. 

…

2 · What the worker holds

Asked over the helix:status message, not by reading caches.keys() — the cache name is a platform implementation detail and apps are deliberately not invited to depend on its format. 

…

3 · Asset vs /_api/me

Go offline and re-run: the asset still answers from cache while /_api/me fails. /_api/* is a root-level platform namespace and the worker's scope can never contain it, so it is structurally unprecachable — which is what makes it a usable reachability probe. 

…

4 · The app's own cache

A cache this app opened itself, with no grant of any kind. This is how you hold a large asset — a model file, a dataset — offline: the platform caches the shell, you cache your payload. Note it is listed separately from the helix: cache and the worker never touches it. 

…

5 · Durable state (IndexedDB)

Also ungranted. Append a few entries, go offline, and hard-reload: the shell cold-boots and the entries are still here. That is the shape of a capture-now-sync-later outbox — the app owns it, the platform never sees it. 

…

6 · Cache version

The cache is keyed to the live version's blob prefix. Promote a new version and reload while online: this changes and the old cache is dropped. Documents are network-first, so an online client always gets the live version — the pointer flip still means what it meant before the worker existed. 

…

Probes 3 and 5 only prove anything with the network actually off — use DevTools → Network → Offline, then hard-reload. See this app's README.
